topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A buffer class owns an array but copies only its raw address. Two objects now believe they own one allocation. A mutation appears in both, and destruction eventually tries to release the same storage twice. The problem is not that copying is bad; the class never defined what a copy should mean.

topics.title: 4.1 Understanding Object Copying
topics.summary: Copy construction creates a new object from an existing object. Copy assignment replaces the value of an object that already exists. Their cleanup responsibilities differ because assignment begins with a live destination that may already own a resource.

This gives the caller an ordinary value model: modifying the copy later does not alter the source. For nontrivial element types, element-copy exceptions and partial construction need additional care; the teaching buffer deliberately stores integers.

blocks.text: A copy constructor initializes a new object from an existing object. At its entry, the destination’s lifetime is being established; there is no old destination value to preserve. The constructor must create a usable new object or fail without leaking any completed resource acquisition. In the buffer, delegated construction allocates storage first, and the copy loop then copies the integer values.

blocks.text: A useful copy-construction test has more than one assertion. Compare size and element values immediately after copying. Mutate the new object and verify the source is unchanged. Then destroy the source while retaining the copy and inspect the surviving values. Each step answers a different question: initial equality, independence, and independent lifetime.

blocks.text: Memberwise copying is not inherently shallow or deep in a useful domain sense. It copies each member according to that member’s semantics. A vector member copies its element values. A shared pointer member copies participation in a shared ownership group. A raw pointer member copies its stored pointer value. Therefore the enclosing record’s semantics emerge from its representation. A class name such as Snapshot cannot turn a shared mutable pointee into an independent value.

blocks.text: Consider graph-shaped data as an extension. Deep copying one node recursively may duplicate shared nodes unintentionally or loop through cycles. A real graph copy needs a policy about identity and sharing, often a mapping from original nodes to their copies. The integer buffer has no such relationships, which is why its copy loop is sufficient for this teaching domain. Do not advertise that loop as a universal deep-copy recipe.

topics.summary: Copy assignment must consider both the incoming value and the destination’s existing allocation. Deleting the destination first and then attempting allocation can lose the old value if the allocation fails. It can also break self-assignment when source and destination are the same object.

blocks.text: The example constructs a temporary copy first. Only after that succeeds does it swap size and storage with the destination. The temporary then destroys the old destination storage. This gives a clear commit point and naturally handles self-assignment, at the cost of allocating a replacement even when existing capacity could potentially be reused.

blocks.text: Copy assignment replaces the value of an already existing destination. Its old resources must eventually be released, but releasing them too early can destroy the only accepted value if allocation of the replacement fails. That distinction from construction is the reason assignment deserves its own design rather than a pasted constructor body.

blocks.text: The candidate-and-swap implementation stages the new value in a temporary buffer. Until that temporary is complete, the destination is untouched. Swapping transfers the old destination into the temporary, whose normal destruction releases it. The swap must exchange every member that participates in the representation invariant. Exchanging storage without the corresponding size would leave both objects internally inconsistent.

blocks.text: The strong exception guarantee has a boundary. Here it means assignment failure leaves the destination buffer’s observable value unchanged. It does not promise that an allocator made no internal bookkeeping changes, that a diagnostic log did not record the attempt, or that an external input stream was rewound. State the relevant observable object rather than writing “nothing changes” without qualification.

blocks.text: Self-assignment is a useful stress case because source and destination name the same object. Candidate-and-swap handles it by making an independent candidate before modifying the destination. A direct self-assignment check can avoid unnecessary work, but it is an optimization after correctness, not a substitute for a sound failure path. Test self-assignment through an alias so the test examines the intended semantics without relying on a compiler to approve an obviously redundant expression.

topics.title: 4.2 Distinguishing Shallow and Deep Copies
topics.summary: “Shallow” and “deep” describe which relationships are duplicated, not a universal ranking of good and bad. Copying a non-owning pointer is a useful shallow observation. Copying an exclusively owning raw pointer as though it created another independent owner is usually a defect.

The defect begins at the ownership model, not at the eventual crash site.

blocks.text: A raw pointer is not always an owner. If both records intentionally borrow a separately owned immutable table, copying the pointer may be exactly right. The owner must outlive both records, and neither record may release it. Avoid teaching “all pointer copying is wrong.” Teach that pointer copying preserves an observation of identity and does not independently duplicate the object or release obligation.

blocks.text: The distinction also appears in standard types. Copying std::string_view copies a view, not the characters. Copying std::span copies an access range, not the underlying array. Copying a shared pointer keeps the same pointee alive through another ownership participant. All of these can be useful when their semantics match the interface. They become defects when an API promises an independent snapshot but returns one of these relationships without naming it.

blocks.text: Independent ownership needs both storage independence and value preservation. Allocate enough storage for the accepted size, copy or construct each element according to its semantics, and establish cleanup for partially completed work. For integer elements, assignment cannot throw and the example is simple. For arbitrary element types, element construction can fail partway through, so a generic container must track and destroy the elements that were actually constructed. This is one reason standard containers are preferable to casually generalized raw-storage exercises.

blocks.text: An assignment can preserve the old value by finishing a candidate before commit. The tradeoff is extra peak memory: both the old allocation and the new allocation can exist simultaneously. A memory-constrained application may select a different guarantee or representation, but it should do so explicitly. Reducing peak memory by overwriting the old buffer in place changes the failure story when element operations can throw.

reading.title: 4.2.2 Implementing Independent Ownership
paragraphs: The buffer uses std::unique_ptr<int[]> internally to ensure each allocation has one release owner. The explicit copy constructor allocates a fresh owned array, so exclusivity remains true while value copying becomes possible at the enclosing type level.

The invariant couples size_ and data_: a positive size must correspond to storage for that many integers; a zero-sized buffer uses an empty pointer. swap exchanges both parts together and is nonthrowing for this representation. Exchanging only one member would violate the invariant even though each individual member remained a valid C++ object.

Independent ownership needs both storage independence and value preservation. Allocate enough storage for the accepted size, copy or construct each element according to its semantics, and establish cleanup for partially completed work. For integer elements, assignment cannot throw and the example is simple. For arbitrary element types, element construction can fail partway through, so a generic container must track and destroy the elements that were actually constructed. This is one reason standard containers are preferable to casually generalized raw-storage exercises.

An assignment can preserve the old value by finishing a candidate before commit. The tradeoff is extra peak memory: both the old allocation and the new allocation can exist simultaneously. A memory-constrained application may select a different guarantee or representation, but it should do so explicitly. Reducing peak memory by overwriting the old buffer in place changes the failure story when element operations can throw.

The supplemental copy-transaction laboratory injects an exception at a chosen copy step. It does not rely on exhausting the machine’s memory. The destination begins with known values, a replacement is attempted, and a specific copy failure is triggered before the swap. The test compares the destination with its earlier snapshot and verifies the source is unchanged. This directly tests the selected commit boundary.

A passing injected-failure test demonstrates the exercised failure points in the laboratory type. It does not prove every allocator or element type has the same guarantees. Keep the custom buffer’s contract narrow, and use standard components when they already express the application’s value semantics.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Delete, then allocate
topics.summary: The naïve assignment first frees the destination’s old allocation, then allocates replacement storage. If the second step fails, the old value has already been destroyed. A catch block cannot recreate it without some other saved copy. Setting the pointer to null avoids a double release but does not restore the promised value. This implementation may support a weaker documented guarantee, but it cannot honestly claim preservation of the previous accepted buffer.
